title: The journeywork of the stars
hookLine: Whitman: a leaf of grass is no less than the journeywork of the stars

cards: A child runs up with two fistfuls of grass and asks: what is it?
That's a scene from Walt Whitman's Song of Myself: "A child said What is the grass? fetching it to me with full hands; how could I answer the child? I do not know what it is any more than he."
A grown man, stumped by a handful of grass. Later in the same poem, he gives an answer you won't find in any botany book.

teach.b: Here it is: "I believe a leaf of grass is no less than the journey-work of the stars, and the pismire is equally perfect, and a grain of sand, and the egg of the wren". First, no less than.
Whitman isn't saying grass is a little bit wonderful. He's saying it equals the stars' own work.
Journeywork is an old craft word for work done by a trained hand, so in Whitman's picture a single blade is something the stars made, and made well. Second, the list keeps going.
The pismire, an old word for an ant, is "equally perfect". So is a grain of sand, which we met with Blake, and the egg of the wren. Whitman piles them up so nothing gets ranked lower.
Third, the next line: "And the tree-toad is a chef-d'oeuvre for the highest". Chef-d'oeuvre is French for masterpiece. And then, "the running blackberry would adorn the parlors of heaven".
A bramble from a ditch, good enough for heaven's living room.
Fourth, the first two words: I believe.
Whitman doesn't claim to have measured this. He states it as belief, just as the child's question got no measured answer.
Wonder, for him, starts with admitting he doesn't know what grass is, and ends with refusing to call any of it small.

how: Readers of Whitman often return to Song of Myself on walks outdoors, and some people on a personal spiritual path use his lists of small creatures as a prompt to look at ordinary living things as finished, careful work.

games.q: a child runs up with two fistfuls of grass and asks you: what is the grass? what does Whitman's speaker say?
o: he admits he knows no more than the child.
he tells the child to go and play.
games.why: "how could I answer the child? I do not know what it is any more than he." the poem's wonder starts with not knowing.

practice: Pick a single blade of grass, or kneel and look at one where it grows; if there's none nearby, a houseplant leaf, a kitchen herb or a weed in a crack will do.
Look at its edges, its veins, the way it narrows to a point, and turn it in the light. No need to think anything grand: just look at it as if someone skilled had made it.

wordCard.voice: Journeywork. An old craft word Whitman used for a leaf of grass: no less than the stars' finished work, and nothing in his list ranked lower. Today's word.
